dx: Sickle cell trait with renal papillary necrosis
case: A 22-year-old man comes to the physician because of 2 days of painless red urine. He plays college basketball and has had no trauma. He takes no regular medications and does not use analgesics. Temperature is 36.8 °C (98.2 °F), pulse 72/min, respirations 14/min, and blood pressure 118/74 mm Hg. Hemoglobin is 14.6 g/dL (13.5 to 17.5), and serum creatinine is 0.9 mg/dL (0.7 to 1.3). Urinalysis shows many red blood cells and no casts, and urine culture shows no growth. After 12 hours of fluid restriction, urine osmolality is 310 mOsm/kg (expected above 800). Hemoglobin electrophoresis shows HbA 58% and HbS 40%. CT urography shows a sloughed left renal papilla. Diagnosis: sickle cell trait with renal papillary necrosis.

questions.stem: His concentrating defect reflects injury to the nephrons whose loops of Henle reach the inner medulla, and to the capillaries that run beside those loops. Which of the following features characterizes these nephrons?
options: Glomeruli in the outer cortex and efferent arterioles forming vasa recta
Glomeruli near the corticomedullary junction and efferent arterioles forming vasa recta
Glomeruli near the corticomedullary junction and short loops ending in the outer medulla
Glomeruli in the outer cortex and long loops reaching the tips of the papillae
approach: Identify the nephrons with loops that reach the inner medulla: juxtamedullary nephrons.
Recall their three features: deep glomeruli, long loops, and efferent arterioles that form the vasa recta.
Link to the case: sickling in the vasa recta damages the countercurrent system these nephrons build, so urine cannot be concentrated.
questions.why: Juxtamedullary nephrons make up a minority of nephrons. Their glomeruli sit near the corticomedullary junction, their loops of Henle dip deep into the inner medulla, and their efferent arterioles give rise to the vasa recta, which run alongside the loops. The long loops build the steep medullary osmotic gradient, and the vasa recta preserve it by countercurrent exchange. When sickled cells block the vasa recta, the gradient is lost and urine osmolality stays near that of plasma (isosthenuria).
whyNot: Outer cortical (superficial) nephrons have efferent arterioles that form peritubular capillaries around cortical tubules. They do not give rise to the vasa recta.
Correct.
Short loops that turn back in the outer medulla belong to cortical nephrons. Juxtamedullary nephrons have the long loops.
Outer cortical nephrons have short loops. The long loops that reach the papillary tips come from glomeruli deep in the cortex.

questions.stem: Chronic analgesic nephropathy produces the same papillary lesion. In that disorder, which of the following best explains why the injury centers on the renal papillae?
options: Immune complexes deposited along the papillary basement membrane
Hypertonic medullary blood promoting polymerization of hemoglobin S
Drug-specific T cells infiltrating the interstitium along with eosinophils
Concentrated toxic metabolites with loss of prostaglandin vasodilation
approach: Name the two parts of classic combination analgesics: phenacetin (or acetaminophen) and aspirin.
Ask why the papilla is vulnerable: drugs are concentrated there, and its blood supply is already marginal.
Combine them: toxic metabolites concentrated in the papilla plus loss of prostaglandin-driven blood flow cause ischemic and oxidative necrosis.
questions.why: The countercurrent system concentrates acetaminophen, the main metabolite of phenacetin, in the inner medulla, where its reactive products deplete glutathione and cause oxidative cell injury. Aspirin and other NSAIDs block prostaglandin synthesis, and the medulla depends on prostaglandins to keep its low blood flow adequate. Together these cause papillary necrosis and chronic interstitial nephritis after years of combination analgesic use. Other causes of papillary necrosis include diabetes mellitus, sickle cell disease and trait, severe acute pyelonephritis, and urinary tract obstruction.
whyNot: Immune complex deposition injures glomeruli and causes glomerulonephritis. It does not explain selective papillary necrosis.
This is the mechanism in this patient. Analgesic nephropathy occurs in people without hemoglobin S.
This describes acute drug-induced interstitial nephritis, a hypersensitivity reaction with fever, rash, and acute kidney injury. It is not the chronic papillary injury of analgesic abuse.
Correct.

questions.stem: His hemoglobin concentration is normal. If repeated injury later progresses to chronic kidney disease with widespread scarring, his anemia would develop mainly from loss of which of the following cells?
options: Peritubular interstitial fibroblasts that sense low oxygen
Juxtaglomerular cells that secrete renin into afferent arterioles
Proximal tubule cells that hydroxylate calcidiol to calcitriol
Macula densa cells that sense sodium chloride in the tubule
approach: Identify the hormone whose loss causes anemia in CKD: erythropoietin.
Recall where it is made: fibroblast-like interstitial cells around the peritubular capillaries of the deep cortex and outer medulla.
Recall the trigger: low tissue oxygen stabilizes HIF, which switches on the erythropoietin gene.
questions.why: Erythropoietin is made by peritubular interstitial fibroblast-like cells in the deep cortex and outer medulla. When oxygen delivery falls, hypoxia-inducible factor is no longer degraded and drives erythropoietin transcription. Erythropoietin keeps erythroid progenitors in the marrow alive and dividing. As CKD destroys these cells, erythropoietin falls and a normocytic, normochromic anemia develops. The opposite happens when a renal cell carcinoma makes erythropoietin, causing secondary polycythemia.
whyNot: Correct.
Juxtaglomerular cells release renin. Their loss or dysfunction affects blood pressure and aldosterone, not red cell production.
Loss of 1-alpha-hydroxylase activity in CKD causes low calcitriol, hypocalcemia, and secondary hyperparathyroidism. It is not the main cause of CKD anemia.
The macula densa senses tubular NaCl for tubuloglomerular feedback and renin release. It does not make erythropoietin.

questions.stem: Which of the following features of the renal medulla most directly explains why red cells sickle there even though he has only about 40% hemoglobin S?
options: High oxygen tension that oxidizes heme iron from the ferrous to ferric form
Rapid blood flow with high shear stress that fragments rigid red blood cells
Low oxygen, high osmolality, and low pH that favor HbS polymerization
Glomerular fenestrae that trap deformed red cells in Bowman space
approach: Recall what makes HbS polymerize: deoxygenation, a higher HbS concentration inside the cell, and acidosis.
Match each to the medulla: countercurrent shunting lowers oxygen, the hypertonic interstitium dehydrates red cells, and the pH is low.
Predict the result: sickling in the vasa recta causes papillary ischemia, hematuria, and loss of concentrating ability.
questions.why: The valine substitution in HbS creates a hydrophobic patch that lets deoxygenated HbS molecules polymerize into rigid fibers. The renal medulla is the one site where conditions favor this even in sickle cell trait. Oxygen tension is low because oxygen diffuses across the hairpin vasa recta, the hypertonic interstitium pulls water out of red cells and raises their HbS concentration, and the acidic pH lowers hemoglobin oxygen affinity. Slow flow keeps cells in this setting longer. Sickled cells occlude the vasa recta, causing hematuria, papillary necrosis, and isosthenuria.
whyNot: The medulla has low oxygen tension. Oxidation of heme iron to the ferric state produces methemoglobin, which is unrelated to sickling.
Blood flow in the vasa recta is slow, not rapid. Shear fragmentation of red cells produces schistocytes in microangiopathic hemolytic anemia.
Correct.
The papillae have no glomeruli. Red cells in the urine here come from infarcted papillae, not from trapping in Bowman space.

dx: Clear cell renal cell carcinoma invading the left renal vein
case: A 61-year-old man comes to the physician because of 3 weeks of intermittent hematuria, a dull left flank ache, and a new left scrotal swelling. He has a 40-pack-year smoking history, hypertension, and obesity. Temperature is 37.1 °C (98.8 °F), pulse 84/min, respirations 16/min, and blood pressure 152/94 mm Hg. A soft mass of dilated veins is palpable above the left testis and does not decompress when he lies supine. Hemoglobin is 18.4 g/dL (13.5 to 17.5), serum calcium is 12.1 mg/dL (8.5 to 10.5), and serum parathyroid hormone is 6 pg/mL (10 to 65). CT shows an 8-cm left renal mass with tumor thrombus extending into the left renal vein. Skeletal imaging shows no bone lesions. Nephrectomy shows a golden-yellow tumor composed of clear cells. Diagnosis: clear cell renal cell carcinoma invading the left renal vein.

questions.stem: Tumor sequencing shows inactivation of both VHL alleles. Which of the following is the most direct consequence of VHL loss in the tumor cells?
options: Failure of WT1 to direct normal nephron differentiation
Loss of tuberin restraint on mTOR growth signaling
Accumulation of HIF that increases VEGF transcription
Release of E2F from retinoblastoma protein control
approach: Recall what VHL protein does: it is part of an E3 ubiquitin ligase that marks HIF-alpha for destruction when oxygen is normal.
Predict the effect of losing it: HIF builds up as if the cell were hypoxic.
Name the target genes: VEGF (angiogenesis), plus PDGF, TGF-alpha, and erythropoietin.
questions.why: VHL is a tumor suppressor on chromosome 3p. In normal oxygen, HIF-alpha is hydroxylated and the VHL ubiquitin ligase complex sends it to the proteasome. When both VHL copies are lost (often by 3p deletion plus a mutation), HIF accumulates and drives transcription of hypoxia genes, most importantly VEGF. This explains why clear cell carcinomas are so vascular. Overproduction of erythropoietin by the same pathway can explain his polycythemia.
whyNot: WT1 loss causes Wilms tumor in children, a tumor of persistent metanephric blastema.
Tuberin is the TSC2 gene product. Its loss activates mTOR and causes angiomyolipomas in tuberous sclerosis.
Correct.
Release of E2F follows loss or inactivation of RB, as in retinoblastoma and osteosarcoma.

topics: Molecular basis of clear cell carcinoma

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains his scrotal finding?
options: Blocked left testicular vein drainage into the left renal vein
Blocked left testicular vein drainage into the inferior vena cava
Blocked left testicular vein drainage into the left internal iliac vein
Blocked testicular lymph drainage to the para-aortic lymph nodes
approach: Recognize the finding: a left varicocele, a dilated pampiniform plexus, that does not empty when supine.
Trace venous drainage: the left testicular vein empties into the left renal vein, which passes between the superior mesenteric artery and the aorta.
Apply to the case: tumor thrombus in the left renal vein raises pressure in the testicular vein and the plexus dilates.
questions.why: The left testicular (gonadal) vein drains into the left renal vein, which passes between the aorta and the superior mesenteric artery to reach the inferior vena cava. Tumor thrombus in the left renal vein raises back pressure in the left testicular vein and dilates the pampiniform plexus. A varicocele that appears suddenly in an older man, or that fails to decompress lying down, suggests venous obstruction by a retroperitoneal or renal mass. Clear cell carcinoma is known for growing into the renal vein.
whyNot: Correct.
The right testicular vein drains directly into the inferior vena cava. The left does not.
The testicular veins do not drain into the internal iliac veins. They ascend through the inguinal canal into the abdomen.
Testicular lymph does drain to para-aortic nodes, but lymphatic obstruction causes scrotal edema or hydrocele, not dilated veins.

questions.stem: If the tumor had instead been composed of papillae with foamy macrophages in their fibrovascular cores, which of the following cytogenetic findings would most likely be present?
options: Deletion of chromosome 11p13 including WT1
Deletion of the short arm of chromosome 3
Hypodiploidy with loss of multiple whole chromosomes
Trisomy of chromosomes 7 and 17
approach: Identify the tumor from the histology: papillae with foamy macrophages means papillary renal cell carcinoma.
Recall its typical cytogenetics: trisomy 7 and 17 (and loss of Y in men).
Contrast the other subtypes: clear cell with 3p loss, chromophobe with hypodiploidy.
questions.why: Papillary renal cell carcinoma is the second most common type. It grows as papillae with fibrovascular cores that often contain foamy macrophages and psammoma bodies, and it is more often multifocal than clear cell carcinoma. Its typical cytogenetic changes are trisomies of chromosomes 7 and 17, and hereditary cases carry activating MET mutations. Clear cell carcinoma shows 3p loss, and chromophobe carcinoma shows loss of whole chromosomes.
whyNot: 11p13 deletion including WT1 is the lesion of Wilms tumor in WAGR syndrome.
Loss of 3p with VHL inactivation is typical of clear cell carcinoma, the tumor in this patient.
Extreme hypodiploidy with loss of whole chromosomes characterizes chromophobe carcinoma, which arises from intercalated cells and has pale cells with perinuclear halos.
Correct.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains his serum calcium concentration?
options: Lytic bone metastases that release calcium from the skeleton
Tumor secretion of parathyroid hormone-related protein
Tumor conversion of calcidiol to 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D
Autonomous hormone secretion from a parathyroid adenoma
approach: Read the PTH: it is low, so the hypercalcemia does not come from the parathyroid glands.
Rule out local bone destruction: skeletal imaging shows no bone lesions.
Conclude: humoral hypercalcemia of malignancy from PTHrP, a classic paraneoplastic product of renal cell carcinoma.
questions.why: Hypercalcemia with suppressed PTH and no bone metastases points to a humoral cause. Renal cell carcinoma can secrete PTH-related protein, which binds the PTH receptor in bone and kidney, increasing bone resorption and renal calcium reabsorption. Standard PTH assays do not detect PTHrP, and the high calcium suppresses native PTH. Renal cell carcinoma also causes polycythemia (erythropoietin) and hypertension (renin), and it spreads by blood to lung and bone. The classic presentation is hematuria, flank pain, and a flank mass.
whyNot: Renal cell carcinoma does produce lytic bone metastases that can raise calcium, but his skeletal imaging shows no bone lesions.
Correct.
Excess 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D production explains hypercalcemia in lymphomas and granulomatous diseases such as sarcoidosis, not renal cell carcinoma.
A parathyroid adenoma would raise serum PTH. His PTH is suppressed, which points away from primary hyperparathyroidism.

topics: Paraneoplastic syndromes of renal cell carcinoma

dx: Von Hippel-Lindau syndrome with bilateral renal cell carcinoma
case: A 29-year-old woman comes to the physician for evaluation of kidney masses found on imaging for abdominal pain. Five years ago, a cerebellar hemangioblastoma was resected. Her father died of kidney cancer at age 44. Temperature is 36.9 °C (98.4 °F), pulse 76/min, respirations 14/min, and blood pressure 124/78 mm Hg. Serum creatinine is 0.8 mg/dL (0.6 to 1.1). MRI shows three solid enhancing masses in the right kidney and two in the left, multiple bilateral renal cysts, and several pancreatic cysts. Partial nephrectomy specimens show clear cell renal cell carcinoma. Germline testing identifies a pathogenic VHL variant. Diagnosis: von Hippel-Lindau syndrome with bilateral renal cell carcinoma.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains why she developed multiple tumors in both kidneys at a young age?
options: Germline loss of one VHL allele, so each tumor needs one more hit
Germline gain-of-function VHL allele acting as a dominant oncogene
Germline loss of both VHL alleles present in every cell from birth
Germline mismatch repair defect that raises the somatic mutation rate
approach: Apply the two-hit model: a tumor suppressor must lose both copies before a cell becomes a tumor.
In the inherited syndrome, every renal tubular cell already carries the first hit.
Any one of millions of cells needs only one somatic hit (often a 3p deletion), so tumors are multiple, bilateral, and early.
questions.why: Von Hippel-Lindau syndrome is autosomal dominant, but at the cellular level the gene acts recessively. Each cell in the body carries one inactive VHL allele from conception. A single somatic event, often deletion of 3p, removes the remaining copy and stabilizes HIF. Because this can happen in many cells, patients develop bilateral, multifocal clear cell carcinomas decades earlier than people with sporadic tumors, who need two somatic hits in the same cell. Hemangioblastomas, pheochromocytomas, and pancreatic cysts arise the same way.
whyNot: Correct.
VHL is a tumor suppressor. Tumors arise from loss of its function, not from a gain of function.
Affected people inherit one mutant allele. Their normal cells keep one working copy and make normal VHL protein until a second hit occurs.
Inherited mismatch repair defects cause Lynch syndrome, with colon, endometrial, and upper urinary tract urothelial cancers, not VHL-type clear cell tumors.

questions.stem: Immunostaining shows that many of her tumor cells have lost surface MHC class I molecules. These tumor cells are most likely to be killed by which of the following?
options: CD4+ T helper 1 lymphocytes
CD8+ cytotoxic T lymphocytes
Natural killer cells
Eosinophils releasing major basic protein
approach: Note the escape strategy: lost MHC class I hides tumor antigens from CD8+ T cells.
Recall which cell watches for missing MHC class I: the NK cell, whose inhibitory receptors bind MHC class I.
Without that inhibitory signal, activating receptors that bind stress ligands trigger killing.
questions.why: CD8+ T cells kill tumor cells by recognizing tumor peptides on MHC class I, so many renal carcinomas downregulate MHC class I to escape them. NK cells cover this gap. Their inhibitory receptors bind self MHC class I, and when MHC class I is missing, signals from activating receptors (such as NKG2D binding stress-induced ligands) dominate. The NK cell then releases perforin and granzymes to kill the target. This is called missing-self recognition.
whyNot: CD4+ T cells recognize peptides on MHC class II, mainly on antigen-presenting cells. They help other cells rather than directly killing MHC class I-negative targets.
CD8+ T cells recognize tumor peptides only when they are presented on MHC class I. Losing MHC class I is a way tumors escape these cells.
Correct.
Eosinophils mainly defend against helminths and drive allergic inflammation. They are not a main defense against tumor cells.

questions.stem: Her kidneys contain many cysts as well as carcinomas. Which of the following other cystic kidney conditions also carries a well-established increased risk of renal cell carcinoma?
options: Autosomal recessive polycystic kidney disease of infancy
Acquired cystic disease of long-term dialysis
Unilateral multicystic dysplastic kidney of the newborn
Medullary sponge kidney with collecting duct ectasia
approach: List the cystic kidney conditions and the setting of each: infancy, congenital malformation, or acquired.
Recall which one develops after years of end-stage kidney disease: acquired cystic disease in dialysis patients.
Recall its key complication: a several-fold increase in renal cell carcinoma.
questions.why: Acquired cystic kidney disease develops in shrunken end-stage kidneys after years of dialysis. Multiple cortical and medullary cysts form, some with atypical lining cells, and the risk of renal cell carcinoma rises several-fold. ARPKD presents in infancy with large spongy kidneys, oligohydramnios, and hepatic fibrosis. Multicystic dysplastic kidney is a noninherited malformation of one kidney with disorganized tissue and cartilage.
whyNot: ARPKD causes bilateral enlarged kidneys in infancy, with Potter sequence and congenital hepatic fibrosis. Kidney cancer is not one of its typical outcomes.
Correct.
Multicystic dysplastic kidney is a noninherited, usually unilateral, developmental malformation. It does not carry a meaningful carcinoma risk, and the other kidney often enlarges to compensate.
Medullary sponge kidney has dilated medullary collecting ducts that predispose to stones and nephrocalcinosis, not to carcinoma.

questions.stem: The resected tumors have a golden-yellow cut surface. Which of the following best explains this gross appearance?
options: Mucin-filled cells derived from the transitional epithelium
Hemosiderin-laden cells derived from medullary collecting ducts
Mitochondria-packed cells derived from intercalated cells
Lipid-rich cytoplasm in cells derived from proximal tubules
approach: Connect the color to cell contents: yellow means lipid.
Connect the clear cytoplasm to lipid and glycogen that dissolve during tissue processing.
Recall the cell of origin of clear cell carcinoma: the proximal tubule.
questions.why: Clear cell renal cell carcinoma arises from proximal tubule epithelium. Its cells store large amounts of lipid and glycogen, which dissolve out during processing and leave clear cytoplasm on slides. The lipid gives the cut surface its golden-yellow color, often mixed with red hemorrhage and gray necrosis. These tumors tend to grow into the renal vein and inferior vena cava. Risk factors include smoking, obesity, hypertension, acquired cystic disease, and VHL syndrome.
whyNot: Mucin-producing glandular tumors of the bladder are adenocarcinomas. Tumors of transitional epithelium are urothelial carcinomas, not yellow renal masses.
Hemosiderin causes brown discoloration in areas of old hemorrhage. Clear cell carcinoma does not arise from medullary collecting ducts.
Mitochondria-packed cells from intercalated cells form oncocytoma, which has a mahogany-brown cut surface.
Correct.

topics: Gross and microscopic features of clear cell carcinoma

case: A 3-year-old boy is brought to the physician because his mother felt a firm mass in his right abdomen while bathing him. He has had absent irises in both eyes since birth, had surgical repair of hypospadias and an undescended testis, and has delayed speech and motor milestones. Temperature is 37.0 °C (98.6 °F), pulse 110/min, respirations 24/min, and blood pressure 128/84 mm Hg (above the 95th percentile for age and height). A smooth, nontender right flank mass does not cross the midline. Urinalysis shows 15 RBC/hpf (0 to 2). Urine catecholamine metabolites are within normal limits. CT shows a large solid mass arising within the right kidney. Diagnosis: Wilms tumor (nephroblastoma) in WAGR syndrome.

questions.stem: Which of the following histologic patterns is most likely in the resected tumor?
options: Spindle cells, mature fat, and thick-walled vessels
Small round blue cells forming Homer Wright rosettes
Clear cells filled with lipid and glycogen
Blastemal, stromal, and epithelial elements
approach: Identify the tumor: an intrarenal mass in a 3-year-old with WAGR features is Wilms tumor.
Recall that Wilms tumor recapitulates the developing kidney.
Name its three components: blastema, stroma, and epithelium (tubules and abortive glomeruli).
questions.why: Wilms tumor is the most common primary renal tumor of childhood, usually seen at 2 to 5 years of age as a large unilateral flank mass, sometimes with hematuria or hypertension. It arises from persistent metanephric tissue and shows a triphasic pattern: sheets of small blue blastemal cells, spindle-cell stroma, and epithelial tubules or glomerulus-like structures. Syndromes that raise the risk include WAGR, Denys-Drash, and Beckwith-Wiedemann.
whyNot: Spindle cells, fat, and thick-walled vessels describe angiomyolipoma, which is linked to tuberous sclerosis.

Small round blue cells in Homer Wright rosettes describe neuroblastoma, a tumor of the adrenal medulla or sympathetic ganglia that often crosses the midline and raises urine catecholamine metabolites.
Clear cells filled with lipid and glycogen describe clear cell renal cell carcinoma, a tumor of older adults.
Correct.

questions.stem: Which of the following genetic findings best explains the combination of features in this child?
options: Loss of imprinting at 11p15 with excess IGF2 expression
Deletion of 11p13 removing WT1 and PAX6
Dominant-negative point mutation in one WT1 allele
Two-hit inactivation of VHL on chromosome 3p
approach: List his features: Wilms tumor, aniridia, genitourinary anomalies, and developmental delay (WAGR).
Ask what single event could cause all of them: loss of several neighboring genes.
Recall the region: 11p13, which holds both WT1 (kidney and gonad) and PAX6 (eye).
questions.why: WAGR syndrome is a contiguous gene deletion at chromosome 11p13. Loss of PAX6 causes aniridia, and loss of WT1 causes genitourinary malformations and a high risk of Wilms tumor once the second WT1 copy is lost in a kidney cell. Additional deleted genes contribute to developmental delay. WT1 encodes a transcription factor needed for normal kidney and gonad development.
whyNot: Loss of imprinting at 11p15 causes Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome, with organomegaly, macroglossia, hemihypertrophy, and omphalocele, not aniridia.
Correct.
A dominant-negative WT1 mutation causes Denys-Drash syndrome, with early nephropathy (diffuse mesangial sclerosis) and gonadal dysgenesis, but not aniridia or developmental delay.
VHL loss causes clear cell renal carcinoma and hemangioblastomas, not childhood Wilms tumor.

questions.stem: His hypertension is attributed to renin released by the tumor. Which of the following sets of plasma findings is most likely?
options: High renin, low aldosterone, and high potassium
Low renin, high aldosterone, and low potassium
High renin, high aldosterone, and low potassium
Low renin, low aldosterone, and high potassium
approach: Start at renin: tumor renin raises it regardless of normal feedback.
Follow the cascade: renin forms angiotensin I, ACE converts it to angiotensin II, and angiotensin II stimulates aldosterone.
Predict aldosterone's effect on principal cells: more sodium reabsorption and more potassium secretion, so potassium falls.
questions.why: Juxtaglomerular cells normally release renin in response to low afferent arteriolar pressure, low NaCl delivery to the macula densa, and beta-1 sympathetic stimulation. Renin cleaves angiotensinogen to angiotensin I, and ACE converts it to angiotensin II, which constricts arterioles and stimulates aldosterone release from the zona glomerulosa. Aldosterone increases sodium reabsorption and potassium secretion in the collecting duct. Atrial natriuretic peptide opposes these effects by inhibiting renin and aldosterone and promoting natriuresis, but it cannot stop renin that a tumor releases on its own.
whyNot: High renin with low aldosterone and hyperkalemia is primary adrenal insufficiency, where the adrenal cannot respond to angiotensin II.
Low renin with high aldosterone is primary hyperaldosteronism, where the adrenal makes aldosterone on its own and suppresses renin.
Correct.
Low renin with low aldosterone and hyperkalemia is hyporeninemic hypoaldosteronism (type 4 renal tubular acidosis), often seen in diabetic nephropathy.

questions.stem: Wilms tumor arises from nephrogenic rests, which are persistent remnants of metanephric blastema. Which of the following best describes when the metanephros first appears and what its blastema normally forms?
options: Week 5; nephrons from Bowman capsule to distal convoluted tubule
Week 5; collecting ducts, minor and major calyces, and renal pelvis
Week 4; a transient kidney whose tubules form the efferent ductules
Week 4; nonfunctional cervical nephrotomes that regress completely
approach: Recall the three kidney systems in order: pronephros, mesonephros, then metanephros.
Place the metanephros: it appears in week 5 and becomes the permanent kidney.
Split its two parts: metanephric blastema forms the nephron, and the ureteric bud forms the collecting system.
questions.why: Three kidney systems form in sequence. The pronephros appears early in week 4 in the cervical region, never functions, and regresses. The mesonephros forms next and works briefly as an interim kidney; its duct and some tubules persist in the male genital tract. The metanephros appears in week 5 and becomes the permanent kidney. Its metanephric blastema forms the nephron from Bowman capsule to the distal convoluted tubule, while the ureteric bud forms the collecting ducts, calyces, pelvis, and ureter.
whyNot: Correct.
Collecting ducts, calyces, and renal pelvis come from the ureteric bud, which grows into the metanephric blastema at about the same time.
This describes the mesonephros, the interim kidney. In males its tubules persist as the efferent ductules of the testis.
This describes the pronephros, a rudimentary structure in the cervical region that never functions and disappears.

dx: Urothelial carcinoma of the bladder in a former dye worker
case: A 66-year-old man comes to the physician because of three episodes of painless gross hematuria over 2 months. For 25 years he worked at a plant that made aniline dyes, handling benzidine and 2-naphthylamine. He smoked 1 pack of cigarettes daily for 30 years and quit 10 years ago. Temperature is 36.7 °C (98.1 °F), pulse 78/min, respirations 14/min, and blood pressure 134/82 mm Hg. Urine cytology shows malignant cells, and urine culture shows no growth. Cystoscopy shows a 3-cm papillary tumor at the bladder dome and separate flat, red, velvety patches on the lateral walls. Biopsies show high-grade papillary urothelial carcinoma invading the detrusor muscle and flat carcinoma in situ in the lateral wall patches. Diagnosis: urothelial carcinoma of the bladder in a former dye worker.

questions.stem: Months later, imaging shows that the tumor at the dome has grown through the bladder wall and its peritoneal covering. When he is upright, tumor cells shed into the peritoneal cavity would most likely collect first in which of the following spaces?
options: Retropubic space
Rectovesical pouch
Hepatorenal recess
Left paracolic gutter
approach: Trace the peritoneum: it covers the superior surface of the bladder, then reflects back onto the rectum.
Name the recess this forms in males: the rectovesical pouch.
Apply gravity: upright, the rectovesical pouch is the lowest point of the male peritoneal cavity.
questions.why: Only the superior surface of the bladder is covered by peritoneum. In males, the peritoneum passes from the bladder back onto the anterior rectum and forms the rectovesical pouch, the lowest part of the peritoneal cavity in the upright position. Fluid, blood, pus, or shed tumor cells collect there first. In females, the uterus sits between bladder and rectum, creating a vesicouterine pouch in front and a rectouterine pouch behind, and the rectouterine pouch is lowest.
whyNot: The retropubic space lies in front of the bladder, outside the peritoneum. Cells shed into the peritoneal cavity cannot reach it.
Correct.
The hepatorenal recess is the lowest part of the upper abdominal peritoneal cavity when a person lies supine. Upright, fluid falls into the pelvis.
The paracolic gutters carry fluid between the upper abdomen and pelvis. They are pathways, not the lowest collecting point.

questions.stem: During transurethral resection of the dome tumor, the bladder is distended with irrigation fluid, and the resectoscope perforates the full thickness of the dome. Where will the irrigation fluid most likely collect?
options: Peritoneal cavity
Retropubic space of Retzius
Superficial perineal space
Perirenal fat within renal fascia
approach: Locate the perforation: the dome, the only bladder surface covered by peritoneum.
Recall that a distended bladder rises into the abdomen, so the dome lies against the peritoneal cavity.
Predict: a dome breach leaks into the peritoneal cavity, while breaches elsewhere stay extraperitoneal.
questions.why: The kidneys and ureters are retroperitoneal, and the bladder is extraperitoneal with only its superior surface (the dome) covered by peritoneum. When the bladder is full, the dome rises above the pubis into the abdomen. A tear through the dome, whether from instruments or a blow to a full bladder, leaks urine or fluid into the peritoneal cavity. By contrast, bladder injuries with pelvic fractures usually tear the anterior or lateral wall and leak into the extraperitoneal perivesical and retropubic spaces.
whyNot: Correct.
Fluid enters the retropubic space when the anterior or lateral bladder wall is breached below the peritoneum, as in extraperitoneal rupture with pelvic fracture.
The superficial perineal space fills when the spongy urethra is torn, as in a straddle injury. A bladder dome injury does not reach it.
The perirenal space surrounds the kidney within renal fascia. Fluid from the bladder dome does not track there.

questions.stem: The invasive tumor is surrounded by CD8+ T cells, and the tumor cells strongly express PD-L1. Which of the following best explains how this expression allows the tumor to escape the T cells?
options: Replaces MHC class II, which CD8+ T cells need for recognition
Binds CD28 on T cells and delivers a costimulatory signal
Binds CTLA-4 on T cells and delivers an activating signal
Binds PD-1 on T cells and delivers an inhibitory signal
approach: Identify the ligand-receptor pair: PD-L1 on tumor cells binds PD-1 on activated T cells.
Recall what PD-1 signaling does: it dampens T-cell receptor signaling and leads to T-cell exhaustion.
Apply: tumor-specific CD8+ T cells are present but switched off.
questions.why: Chronically stimulated T cells express PD-1. When PD-1 binds PD-L1 on tumor cells, it recruits phosphatases that dampen T-cell receptor signaling, so CD8+ T cells stop killing and become exhausted. Tumors can also escape by reducing MHC class I so CD8+ T cells cannot see their antigens. Antibodies that block PD-1 or PD-L1 release this brake, which is why urothelial and renal carcinomas can respond to checkpoint blockade.
whyNot: CD8+ T cells recognize peptide on MHC class I, not MHC class II.
CD28 binds B7 molecules (CD80 and CD86) on antigen-presenting cells and provides the second signal that activates T cells. This would strengthen the attack.
CTLA-4 binds B7 molecules and is an inhibitory receptor, not an activating one. PD-L1 does not use CTLA-4.
Correct.

questions.stem: After complete resection, he is scheduled for repeat cystoscopy every few months for years. Which of the following best explains the need for this surveillance?
options: Urothelial carcinoma typically recurs as squamous cell carcinoma
Low-grade papillary tumors almost always progress to invasive disease
Carcinogens in urine have injured the entire urothelial surface
Aromatic amines remain stored within the detrusor muscle for decades
approach: Note his exposures: aromatic amine dyes and smoking, both excreted as carcinogens in urine.
Recall that urine bathes the whole urothelium from renal pelvis to urethra.
Conclude: the whole lining is at risk (field effect), so new tumors keep appearing in other sites.
questions.why: Urothelial carcinoma presents with painless hematuria and is often multifocal. Carcinogens from smoking, aromatic amines such as benzidine and 2-naphthylamine, cyclophosphamide, and phenacetin are excreted in urine and expose the entire urothelium. This field effect explains frequent new tumors after resection, sometimes in the ureter or renal pelvis. Two precursor routes exist: papillary tumors, which recur often, and flat carcinoma in situ, which is high grade and more likely to invade.
whyNot: Recurrences are usually urothelial carcinoma again. Squamous cell carcinoma of the bladder is linked to chronic irritation such as schistosomiasis.
Low-grade papillary tumors recur often but seldom invade. Progression is the main risk of high-grade tumors and flat carcinoma in situ.
Correct.
Aromatic amines act through contact with urine. They are not stored in the bladder muscle.

dx: Squamous cell carcinoma of the bladder with Schistosoma haematobium infection
case: A 47-year-old woman comes to the physician because of 4 months of intermittent blood in the urine, urinary frequency, and burning with urination. She grew up in a farming village in the Nile Delta and moved to the United States 3 years ago. Temperature is 37.0 °C (98.6 °F), pulse 80/min, respirations 14/min, and blood pressure 126/80 mm Hg. Hemoglobin is 11.2 g/dL (12.0 to 16.0). Urine microscopy shows red blood cells and large oval eggs with a sharp terminal spine. A plain radiograph shows calcification outlining the bladder wall. Cystoscopy shows an ulcerated mass on the posterosuperior bladder wall. Biopsy shows keratinizing squamous cell carcinoma, with calcified eggs in the surrounding bladder wall. Diagnosis: squamous cell carcinoma of the bladder with Schistosoma haematobium infection.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains the histologic type of her tumor?
options: Aromatic amine injury to otherwise normal urothelial cells
Glandular metaplasia arising in a persistent urachal remnant
Squamous metaplasia from chronic egg-induced inflammation
Intestinal-type epithelium persisting after bladder exstrophy
approach: Note the tumor type: keratinizing squamous cell carcinoma, which is uncommon in the bladder.
Find the chronic irritant: schistosome eggs trapped in the bladder wall.
Link irritation to cancer: chronic inflammation leads to squamous metaplasia, then dysplasia, then carcinoma.
questions.why: Schistosoma haematobium eggs lodge in the bladder wall and provoke granulomatous inflammation, fibrosis, and calcification. Years of chronic irritation convert the urothelium to squamous epithelium (metaplasia), which can become dysplastic and then invasive squamous cell carcinoma. Other chronic irritants such as stones and long-term catheters do the same. Bladder adenocarcinoma instead arises from urachal remnants or exstrophy.
whyNot: Aromatic amines cause urothelial carcinoma, the most common bladder cancer, rather than squamous cell carcinoma.
Urachal remnants give rise to adenocarcinoma at the bladder dome, not keratinizing squamous cell carcinoma.
Correct.
Bladder exstrophy predisposes to adenocarcinoma, not squamous cell carcinoma.

questions.stem: The mass extends through the posterosuperior wall of her bladder. Which of the following spaces lies directly against this surface of her bladder?
options: Retropubic space of Retzius
Rectouterine pouch
Rectovesical pouch
Vesicouterine pouch
approach: Trace the female peritoneum from front to back: over the bladder, onto the uterus, then onto the rectum.
Name the two recesses: vesicouterine in front of the uterus, rectouterine behind it.
Apply: the posterosuperior bladder surface faces the vesicouterine pouch.
questions.why: In females, the peritoneum covering the superior bladder surface reflects onto the anterior uterus, forming the shallow vesicouterine pouch. It then passes over the uterus and down onto the rectum, forming the deeper rectouterine pouch, the lowest part of the female peritoneal cavity. A bladder tumor growing through the posterosuperior wall reaches the vesicouterine pouch and the uterus first.
whyNot: The retropubic space lies in front of the bladder, between it and the pubic bones, and is outside the peritoneum.
The rectouterine pouch lies between the uterus and the rectum, behind the uterus, not against the bladder.
The rectovesical pouch exists only in males, where no uterus separates the bladder from the rectum.
Correct.

questions.stem: CT also shows a 2-cm fluid-filled cyst in the midline of the anterior abdominal wall, between the bladder dome and the umbilicus. This cyst most likely arises from a remnant of which of the following embryonic structures?
options: Allantois
Vitelline duct
Urorectal septum
Mesonephric duct
approach: Locate the cyst: on the path from the bladder apex to the umbilicus.
Recall what runs there in the embryo: the allantois, which becomes the urachus and then the median umbilical ligament.
Predict: incomplete closure leaves a urachal cyst, or a patent urachus that drains urine from the umbilicus.
questions.why: The urorectal septum divides the cloaca into the urogenital sinus in front (which forms the bladder and urethra) and the anorectal canal behind. The allantois connects the bladder apex to the umbilicus and normally closes into a fibrous cord, the urachus, which becomes the median umbilical ligament. If a segment stays open, it forms a urachal cyst. If the whole channel stays open, urine drains from the umbilicus (patent urachus). Urachal remnants are also the source of bladder adenocarcinoma at the dome.
whyNot: Correct.
A persistent vitelline duct causes Meckel diverticulum or a fistula that drains intestinal contents from the umbilicus.
The urorectal septum divides the cloaca. Its failure causes fistulas between the rectum and the urinary tract, not a midline cyst above the bladder.
The mesonephric duct gives rise to the ureteric bud and male genital ducts. Remnants in females form Gartner duct cysts beside the vagina.

questions.stem: She most likely acquired this infection by which of the following routes?
options: Ingestion of eggs in food contaminated with feces
Skin penetration by cercariae from freshwater snails
Ingestion of metacercariae in undercooked freshwater fish
Bite of a blackfly that deposits infective larvae
approach: Identify the parasite: a terminal-spined egg in urine is Schistosoma haematobium.
Recall the life cycle: eggs hatch in fresh water, miracidia infect snails, and snails release cercariae.
Apply: cercariae penetrate the skin of people who wade or bathe in that water.
questions.why: Schistosoma haematobium eggs pass in urine and hatch in fresh water into miracidia, which infect specific snails. The snails release free-swimming cercariae that penetrate human skin during contact with the water. The larvae travel through the circulation, mature in the portal system, and the adult worm pairs settle in the vesical venous plexus. Their terminal-spined eggs work through the bladder wall, causing hematuria, fibrosis, calcification, and in time squamous cell carcinoma.
whyNot: Ingesting eggs from fecal contamination transmits Ascaris, Trichuris, and Taenia solium cysticercosis, not schistosomes.
Correct.
Metacercariae in raw or undercooked freshwater fish transmit the liver fluke Clonorchis sinensis.
Blackfly bites transmit Onchocerca volvulus, which causes river blindness.

case: A 32-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department because of sudden severe left flank pain for 3 hours. She has had seizures since early childhood. Temperature is 37.2 °C (99.0 °F), pulse 112/min, respirations 20/min, and blood pressure 98/62 mm Hg. Examination shows facial angiofibromas, several hypopigmented macules on the trunk, and a periungual fibroma. Hemoglobin is 8.9 g/dL (12.0 to 16.0). CT shows multiple bilateral renal masses containing fat density, the largest a 9-cm left renal mass with surrounding retroperitoneal hemorrhage, and numerous bilateral renal cysts. Biopsy of a smaller mass shows thick-walled blood vessels, smooth muscle, and mature fat. Diagnosis: renal angiomyolipomas in tuberous sclerosis complex.

questions.stem: Her renal cysts are unusually numerous and enlarging. Genetic testing shows a large deletion on chromosome 16p that removes TSC2 and the gene immediately next to it. The neighboring gene most likely encodes which of the following proteins?
options: Hamartin
Polycystin-2
Fibrocystin
Polycystin-1
approach: Locate TSC2: chromosome 16p13.3.
Recall which polycystic kidney gene lies on the same arm: PKD1, encoding polycystin-1.
Apply: a deletion removing both genes causes tuberous sclerosis with severe, early polycystic kidney disease.
questions.why: PKD1 lies right next to TSC2 on chromosome 16p13.3, so a large deletion can remove both, producing tuberous sclerosis plus severe early polycystic kidneys. Polycystin-1 (PKD1) and polycystin-2 (PKD2, chromosome 4) work together in primary cilia of tubular cells to regulate calcium signaling and cell growth, and loss leads to cyst formation. Both are autosomal dominant: each child of an affected parent has a 50% risk. PKD1 accounts for most families and causes earlier kidney failure than PKD2. ARPKD from PKHD1 (fibrocystin) skips generations and appears in infancy.
whyNot: Hamartin is the TSC1 product, encoded on chromosome 9, not 16.
Polycystin-2 is encoded by PKD2 on chromosome 4. PKD2 disease is autosomal dominant but milder and later in onset.
Fibrocystin is encoded by PKHD1 on chromosome 6 and causes autosomal recessive polycystic kidney disease in infants.
Correct.

questions.stem: To stop the bleeding, the segmental artery branch supplying the largest tumor is embolized. Which of the following is most likely to develop in the kidney tissue supplied by that branch?
options: Wedge-shaped cortical infarct with its base at the capsule
Diffuse bilateral cortical necrosis sparing the medulla
Normal perfusion through arcuate artery anastomoses
Patchy necrosis of the papillae sparing the overlying cortex
approach: Recall that segmental, interlobar, and arcuate arteries do not anastomose: they are end arteries.
Predict that occluding one branch kills all the tissue it supplies.
Picture the shape: the territory fans out from the hilum, so the infarct is a wedge with its base at the capsule.
questions.why: Each renal segmental artery supplies its own segment with no meaningful collateral flow from neighbors, and the interlobar and arcuate arteries behave the same way. Embolic occlusion, whether therapeutic or from a cardiac embolus, therefore causes a pale coagulative infarct of the whole territory. Because the vessels fan out toward the surface, the infarct is wedge-shaped, with its apex toward the hilum and its base at the capsule. A thin rim just under the capsule may survive on capsular collateral vessels.
whyNot: Correct.
Diffuse bilateral cortical necrosis follows shock or disseminated intravascular coagulation, which affect both kidneys at once. A single embolized branch affects one territory.
Arcuate arteries do not form effective anastomoses with one another, so they cannot keep the tissue perfused.
Papillary necrosis follows analgesic abuse, sickle cell disease, diabetes, or obstruction. Arterial occlusion damages the whole wedge of tissue that the artery supplies.

topics: Renal segmental arteries as end arteries

questions.stem: A separate 4-cm mass without fat is removed from her right kidney. It is mahogany brown with a central stellate scar, and electron microscopy shows tumor cells packed with mitochondria. Which of the following best describes this lesion?
options: Malignant papillary tumor with trisomy of chromosomes 7 and 17
Malignant tumor of intercalated cells with perinuclear halos
Benign tumor of collecting duct intercalated cells
Malignant tumor of lipid-laden proximal tubule cells
approach: Note the clues: mahogany brown, central stellate scar, and cells packed with mitochondria.
Name the tumor: oncocytoma.
Recall its behavior: benign, arising from intercalated cells of the collecting duct.
questions.why: Oncocytoma is a benign renal tumor of large eosinophilic cells whose cytoplasm is packed with mitochondria. Grossly it is tan to mahogany brown, often with a central stellate scar. It arises from intercalated cells of the collecting duct, like chromophobe carcinoma, but does not metastasize. Chromophobe carcinoma has pale cells with prominent borders and perinuclear halos, papillary carcinoma shows trisomy 7 and 17, and clear cell carcinoma has lipid-rich proximal tubule cells.
whyNot: Papillary renal cell carcinoma forms papillae with foamy macrophages, not a brown mass with a central scar.
Pale cells with distinct cell borders and perinuclear halos describe chromophobe carcinoma, a malignant tumor with a good prognosis.
Correct.
Lipid-laden proximal tubule cells form clear cell carcinoma, which has a golden-yellow cut surface.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains the overgrowth of her renal tumors at the molecular level?
options: Stabilization of HIF after loss of VHL ubiquitin ligase
Loss of tuberin-hamartin inhibition of mTOR signaling
Loss of WT1 control of nephron differentiation
Activating mutation in the MET receptor tyrosine kinase
approach: Identify the syndrome: tuberous sclerosis, from TSC1 (hamartin) or TSC2 (tuberin) mutation.
Recall what the complex does: it inactivates Rheb, the activator of mTORC1.
Predict loss: mTORC1 is always on, driving cell growth and hamartomas such as angiomyolipomas.
questions.why: Hamartin (TSC1, chromosome 9) and tuberin (TSC2, chromosome 16) form a complex that acts as a GTPase-activating protein for Rheb. Keeping Rheb in its inactive GDP-bound state holds mTORC1 in check. When the second allele of either gene is lost in a cell, Rheb stays active and mTORC1 drives protein synthesis and cell growth. This produces hamartomas: renal angiomyolipomas (blood vessels, smooth muscle, fat), cortical tubers, cardiac rhabdomyomas, and renal cysts.
whyNot: HIF stabilization from VHL loss drives clear cell renal carcinoma and hemangioblastomas in von Hippel-Lindau syndrome.
Correct.
WT1 loss causes Wilms tumor, a childhood tumor of nephrogenic blastema.
Activating MET mutations cause hereditary papillary renal cell carcinoma.

case: A 20-year-old woman comes to the student health clinic because of 2 days of burning with urination, urinary frequency, urgency, and lower abdominal discomfort. She became sexually active with a new partner 1 week ago. Temperature is 37.0 °C (98.6 °F), pulse 78/min, respirations 14/min, and blood pressure 112/70 mm Hg. Mild suprapubic tenderness is present, and there is no costovertebral angle tenderness. Urinalysis shows positive leukocyte esterase, negative nitrite, 40 WBC/hpf (0 to 5), and 8 RBC/hpf (0 to 2). Urine culture grows more than 100,000 CFU/mL of catalase-positive, coagulase-negative, gram-positive cocci in clusters that are resistant to novobiocin. Diagnosis: acute cystitis due to Staphylococcus saprophyticus.

questions.stem: Which of the following additional findings would most strongly indicate that her infection has ascended to the kidney?
options: White blood cell casts in the urine sediment
Positive nitrite reaction on urine dipstick
Tenderness to palpation above the pubic symphysis
Gross hematuria with small blood clots
approach: Separate lower from upper tract findings: dysuria, frequency, urgency, and suprapubic pain without fever fit cystitis.
Ask which urine finding can only form in the kidney: casts, which are molded in renal tubules.
Conclude: white cell casts show inflammation in the renal parenchyma, as in pyelonephritis.
questions.why: Casts form when Tamm-Horsfall protein gels inside renal tubules and traps cells, so a white cell cast proves that leukocytes were in the tubules. In a patient with urinary tract infection, this means pyelonephritis. Clinically, pyelonephritis adds fever, flank pain, and costovertebral angle tenderness to bladder symptoms. Risk factors for cystitis include female sex, sexual intercourse, pregnancy, catheters, diabetes, and obstruction.
whyNot: Correct.
Nitrite shows nitrate-reducing gram-negative bacteria such as E. coli. It is common in simple cystitis and does not tell where the infection is.
Suprapubic tenderness is a sign of bladder inflammation, which she already has.
Gross hematuria can occur in hemorrhagic cystitis. Blood in the urine does not place the infection in the kidney.

questions.stem: As her bladder fills between voids, its lining stretches while still keeping urine out of the bladder wall. Which of the following changes in the epithelium makes this possible?
options: A surface layer of keratin thickens to resist the increase in wall tension
Basal cells divide rapidly to add extra layers of epithelium during filling
Tight junctions between surface cells open to allow passive stretching
Umbrella cells flatten and add uroplakin plaques to their apical membrane
approach: Identify the epithelium: transitional epithelium (urothelium) with large surface umbrella cells.
Recall the two jobs: stretch during filling and block urine from leaking in.
Link structure to function: umbrella cells flatten and insert stored uroplakin plaques into their surface, while tight junctions and plaques keep the barrier.
questions.why: The urothelium has basal cells, intermediate cells, and a surface layer of large umbrella cells. The apical membrane of umbrella cells contains stiff uroplakin plaques that are very impermeable to water and solutes, and tight junctions seal the gaps between cells. During filling, umbrella cells flatten and insert extra plaque-containing membrane from cytoplasmic vesicles, enlarging their surface without breaking the barrier. Beneath lie the lamina propria and the smooth muscle detrusor.
whyNot: Normal urothelium is not keratinized. Keratinization appears only after squamous metaplasia, as with chronic irritation.
Cell division is far too slow to follow minute-to-minute filling. The urothelium actually becomes thinner as it stretches.
Opening tight junctions would let urine leak into the bladder wall. The tight junctions stay sealed and are part of the barrier.
Correct.

questions.stem: Which of the following anatomic features most directly explains why women have a higher risk of this infection than men?
options: Absence of a trigone at the base of the bladder
Short urethra that opens near the vaginal introitus
Ureters that enter the bladder wall at a right angle
Wider ureteric orifices at the corners of the trigone
approach: Recall the route of most cystitis: bacteria from the perineum ascend through the urethra.
Compare lengths: the female urethra is about 4 cm, and the male urethra is much longer, with prostatic, membranous, and spongy parts.
Conclude: a short urethra opening near the vagina and anus gives bacteria an easy path, and intercourse pushes them inward.
questions.why: The female urethra is about 4 cm long and opens into the vestibule just in front of the vaginal opening, close to perineal and fecal flora. Bacteria colonize the periurethral area and reach the bladder over a short distance, helped by intercourse. The male urethra runs much farther through the prostate, the external sphincter (membranous part), and the corpus spongiosum, so ascending infection is far less common in men.
whyNot: Both sexes have a trigone, the smooth triangle between the two ureteric orifices and the internal urethral orifice.
Correct.
The ureters pass obliquely through the bladder wall in both sexes. A short or perpendicular course causes vesicoureteral reflux, not a sex difference in cystitis.
The ureteric orifices are similar in both sexes. Their shape affects reflux, not entry of bacteria from the perineum.

questions.stem: Escherichia coli, the most common cause of this condition, attaches to bladder urothelium mainly through which of the following?
options: K1 capsule blocking complement deposition
P fimbriae binding glycolipids of the renal pelvis
Type 1 fimbriae binding mannose on uroplakins
Shiga-like toxin binding endothelial Gb3
approach: Recall uropathogenic E. coli: a gram-negative, lactose-fermenting rod from fecal flora.
Match the adhesin to the site: type 1 fimbriae for the bladder, P fimbriae for the kidney.
Name the receptor: the FimH tip binds mannose on uroplakins of umbrella cells.
questions.why: Uropathogenic E. coli comes from the patient's own fecal flora and causes most urinary tract infections. Its type 1 fimbriae carry the FimH adhesin, which binds mannose residues on uroplakin proteins of umbrella cells and lets the bacteria resist being flushed out, causing cystitis. Strains with P fimbriae bind glycolipids on upper urinary tract epithelium and are more likely to cause pyelonephritis. Staphylococcus saprophyticus is the second most common cause in young sexually active women.
whyNot: The K1 capsule resists phagocytosis and complement and is linked to neonatal meningitis. It is not an adhesin.
P fimbriae bind galactose-containing glycolipids on upper tract epithelium. They are linked to pyelonephritis rather than cystitis.
Correct.
Shiga-like toxin from enterohemorrhagic E. coli damages endothelium in hemolytic uremic syndrome. It does not attach bacteria to the bladder.

dx: Catheter-associated Pseudomonas cystitis with neurogenic bladder after spinal cord injury
case: A 34-year-old man with a complete spinal cord injury at the T6 level from a motorcycle crash 2 years ago comes to the clinic because of cloudy, foul-smelling urine and increased leg spasms for 3 days. He has used an indwelling urethral catheter since an episode of urinary retention 6 months ago. Earlier urodynamic testing showed involuntary detrusor contractions at low bladder volumes with simultaneous contraction of the external urethral sphincter. Temperature is 37.3 °C (99.1 °F), pulse 76/min, respirations 14/min, and blood pressure 122/78 mm Hg. Urinalysis shows positive leukocyte esterase and 60 WBC/hpf (0 to 5). Urine culture grows more than 100,000 CFU/mL of Pseudomonas aeruginosa. Diagnosis: catheter-associated Pseudomonas cystitis with neurogenic bladder after spinal cord injury.

questions.stem: His urodynamic findings result from loss of descending input from which of the following structures?
options: Sacral parasympathetic nucleus at S2 to S4
Pontine micturition center
Pudendal nerve motor fibers to the sphincter
Sympathetic neurons of the T11 to L2 cord
approach: Place the lesion: T6, above the sacral cord, so the sacral reflex arc still works.
Explain the contractions: bladder stretch triggers a sacral reflex to the detrusor, giving a reflex (spastic) bladder.
Explain the sphincter contracting at the same time: the pons normally relaxes the sphincter when the detrusor contracts, and that signal is cut off.
questions.why: Normal voiding is coordinated by the pontine micturition center. When it fires, sacral parasympathetic neurons (S2 to S4, pelvic splanchnic nerves) contract the detrusor while pudendal motor neurons and sympathetic outflow to the bladder neck are inhibited, so the sphincters relax. A cord lesion above the sacral segments leaves the sacral reflex intact but cuts the pons off, producing a reflex bladder with detrusor-sphincter dyssynergia, high pressures, and incomplete emptying. A lesion at the sacral cord or cauda equina destroys the reflex arc and causes a flaccid bladder with overflow.
whyNot: The sacral parasympathetic neurons lie below his injury and are intact. They are producing the reflex detrusor contractions.
Correct.
The pudendal nerve is a peripheral nerve from the sacral cord. It is intact, which is why the external sphincter can contract.
These sympathetic neurons lie below his injury and are intact. They relax the detrusor and close the internal sphincter during filling.

questions.stem: The involuntary detrusor contractions on his earlier study share their mechanism with which of the following types of incontinence in neurologically intact adults?
options: Overflow incontinence
Stress incontinence
Urge incontinence
Functional incontinence
approach: Identify the mechanism: involuntary detrusor contractions, also called detrusor overactivity.
Recall which incontinence type has this mechanism: urge incontinence, with sudden urgency and leakage.
Contrast the others: stress means weak urethral support, and overflow means poor emptying.
questions.why: Urge incontinence results from detrusor overactivity: the bladder contracts before the person chooses to void, producing sudden urgency and leakage. Stress incontinence results from weak pelvic floor and urethral support, often after childbirth and with a cystocele, so rises in abdominal pressure push urine out. Overflow incontinence results from a bladder that cannot empty because of an underactive detrusor or an obstruction.
whyNot: Overflow incontinence comes from an underactive detrusor or outlet obstruction, as with prostatic enlargement or a sacral cord lesion. The overfull bladder dribbles.
Stress incontinence comes from weak urethral support or sphincter weakness, as after vaginal deliveries or with a cystocele. Leakage happens with coughing or lifting, without detrusor contraction.
Correct.
Functional incontinence occurs when a person with a normal bladder cannot reach the toilet in time because of limited mobility or cognition.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains why an indwelling catheter allows this infection to persist?
options: Continuous bladder distension that disrupts the urothelial barrier
Catheter-induced loss of IgA secretion by the bladder urothelium
Hematogenous seeding of the bladder wall from a distant skin site
Biofilm on the catheter that resists antibiotics and phagocytes
approach: Recall why catheters are a major cystitis risk factor: they bypass urethral defenses and provide a surface for bacteria.
Recall what Pseudomonas does on plastic: it makes an alginate-rich biofilm.
Apply: bacteria inside biofilm grow slowly and are shielded, so the infection resists clearance.
questions.why: Catheters let bacteria climb along the inner and outer surfaces of the tube, past the urethral defenses. Pseudomonas and other organisms attach and secrete a slimy matrix (for Pseudomonas, largely alginate) that forms a biofilm. Bacteria within biofilm are shielded from antibodies, phagocytes, and many antibiotics and keep reseeding the urine. The risk of bacteriuria rises with each day the catheter stays in. Incomplete emptying from neurogenic bladder adds to the risk.
whyNot: An indwelling catheter drains the bladder continuously, so it prevents distension rather than causing it.
There is no established loss of IgA secretion from catheters. The main problem is the foreign surface and the bypassed urethral defenses.
Bacteria reach the catheterized bladder by ascending along the catheter, not through the bloodstream.
Correct.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes the laboratory features of the organism isolated from his urine?
options: Oxidase-positive gram-negative rod that does not ferment lactose
Oxidase-negative gram-negative rod with a mucoid lactose-fermenting colony
Catalase-negative gram-positive coccus that grows in 6.5% sodium chloride
Coagulase-negative gram-positive coccus that resists novobiocin
approach: Identify the organism: Pseudomonas aeruginosa.
Recall its key traits: gram-negative rod, oxidase-positive, and non-lactose-fermenting, often with blue-green pigment and a grape-like odor.
Rule out the other urinary pathogens by their traits.
questions.why: Pseudomonas aeruginosa is an aerobic gram-negative rod that is oxidase-positive and does not ferment lactose, which separates it from E. coli and Klebsiella. Colonies often make blue-green pigments such as pyocyanin and smell like grapes. It thrives in moist hospital settings and on devices, so it is a classic cause of catheter-associated urinary infection. It is also a major pathogen in burns and cystic fibrosis.
whyNot: Correct.
A mucoid, lactose-fermenting, oxidase-negative rod describes Klebsiella pneumoniae, which has a thick polysaccharide capsule.
A catalase-negative coccus that grows in 6.5% NaCl and bile describes Enterococcus, a common cause of urinary infection in catheterized and hospitalized patients.
A coagulase-negative, novobiocin-resistant coccus describes Staphylococcus saprophyticus, which causes cystitis in young sexually active women.

case: A 23-year-old man comes to the physician because of 4 days of burning with urination and a thick yellow urethral discharge, followed by 1 day of right scrotal pain and swelling. He has had two new female sexual partners in the past month and uses condoms inconsistently. He was treated for gonorrhea 2 years ago. Temperature is 38.1 °C (100.6 °F), pulse 92/min, respirations 16/min, and blood pressure 124/76 mm Hg. The right epididymis is swollen and tender, the right testis lies in a normal position, and the cremasteric reflex is present. Nucleic acid amplification testing of urine is positive for Neisseria gonorrhoeae and negative for Chlamydia trachomatis. Diagnosis: gonococcal urethritis with right epididymitis.

questions.stem: Four years ago, he fell astride a metal fence rail and developed blood at the urethral meatus and bruising of the perineum. Which part of the urethra was most likely torn in that injury?
options: Prostatic urethra
Membranous urethra
Bulbous part of the spongy urethra
Pendulous part of the spongy urethra
approach: Identify the mechanism: a straddle injury crushes the perineum against the pubic arch.
Find the urethral segment fixed in the perineum below the pubic arch: the bulbous part of the spongy urethra.
Contrast with pelvic fracture, which tears the membranous urethra.
questions.why: In a straddle injury, the bulbous part of the spongy urethra is crushed against the inferior pubic rami. Blood and urine escape into the superficial perineal space, deep to the membranous layer of superficial fascia (Colles fascia), and spread into the scrotum, penis, and lower abdominal wall but not the thighs. Pelvic fractures instead tear the posterior urethra at the membranous segment, often with a high-riding prostate and extravasation into the retropubic space.
whyNot: The prostatic urethra is protected within the prostate and is rarely torn by blunt injury.
The membranous urethra is torn by pelvic fractures, which shear it where it passes through the deep perineal pouch below the prostate.
Correct.
The pendulous (penile) urethra is mobile and lies in front of the pubic arch, so it is not crushed against bone in a straddle fall.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains why his infection 2 years ago did not protect him from this one?
options: Obligate intracellular replication within host cells
Antigenic variation of pilin proteins
Polysaccharide capsule that blocks opsonization
Protein A binding the Fc portion of IgG
approach: Identify the organism: Neisseria gonorrhoeae, a gram-negative diplococcus.
Ask what lets it reinfect the same person: changing its main surface antigens.
Recall the mechanism: recombination of pilin genes changes pilus antigens, so old antibodies no longer bind.
questions.why: Gonococcal pili attach the organism to urethral and cervical epithelium. The pilin gene recombines with many silent copies, so the pili keep changing their antigens, and outer membrane Opa proteins switch on and off. Antibodies from an earlier infection no longer match, which allows repeated infections and has prevented a vaccine. Gonococci also make IgA protease, which cleaves mucosal IgA. Nucleic acid amplification testing is the standard diagnostic test for both gonorrhea and chlamydia.
whyNot: Obligate intracellular growth with elementary and reticulate bodies describes Chlamydia trachomatis, not Neisseria gonorrhoeae.
Correct.
Neisseria gonorrhoeae lacks a polysaccharide capsule. Neisseria meningitidis has one, which is why a meningococcal vaccine works.
Protein A is a Staphylococcus aureus surface protein. Gonococci do not make it.

questions.stem: Bacteria most likely reached his epididymis by ascending through ducts that open into which segment of the urethra?
options: Prostatic urethra
Membranous urethra
Bulbous part of the spongy urethra
Navicular fossa of the spongy urethra
approach: Trace the path in reverse: epididymis, ductus deferens, ejaculatory duct, urethra.
Recall where the ejaculatory ducts open: on the seminal colliculus in the prostatic urethra.
Conclude: urethral organisms reach the epididymis by climbing back up through the ejaculatory duct and ductus deferens.
questions.why: The male urethra has prostatic, membranous, and spongy segments. The ejaculatory ducts, formed by the ductus deferens joining the seminal vesicle duct, open on the seminal colliculus of the prostatic urethra, along with the prostatic ducts. Organisms from urethritis can ascend this route to cause epididymitis. In sexually active men younger than about 35 years, epididymitis is usually caused by Neisseria gonorrhoeae or Chlamydia trachomatis.
whyNot: Correct.
The membranous urethra is the short segment passing through the external sphincter. No genital ducts open into it.
The ducts of the bulbourethral glands open into the bulbous part of the spongy urethra. These glands do not connect to the epididymis.
The navicular fossa is the dilated end of the urethra in the glans. No ducts from the epididymis open there.

questions.stem: One of his partners has an untreated endocervical infection with the same organism. Which of the following complications is she at greatest risk of developing?
options: Bacterial vaginosis with clue cells
Squamous cell carcinoma of the cervix
Toxic shock syndrome
Salpingitis with tubal scarring
approach: Recall that gonococcal cervicitis can ascend through the uterus to the fallopian tubes.
Name the result: pelvic inflammatory disease with salpingitis.
Predict the long-term effect: tubal scarring, causing infertility and ectopic pregnancy.
questions.why: Untreated gonococcal or chlamydial cervicitis can ascend to the endometrium and fallopian tubes, causing pelvic inflammatory disease with salpingitis and sometimes tubo-ovarian abscess. Scarring of the tubes leads to infertility and ectopic pregnancy. Gonococcal urethritis gives a purulent discharge with gram-negative intracellular diplococci, while nongonococcal urethritis (often Chlamydia trachomatis) gives scant discharge. Other complications include epididymitis, disseminated gonococcal infection with septic arthritis, and reactive arthritis after chlamydial infection.
whyNot: Bacterial vaginosis is an overgrowth of Gardnerella and anaerobes with clue cells and a fishy odor. It is not caused by gonococci.
Cervical squamous cell carcinoma is caused by high-risk human papillomavirus, not gonorrhea.
Toxic shock syndrome comes from Staphylococcus aureus or Streptococcus pyogenes toxins acting as superantigens.
Correct.
